title: PepCompass: Navigating Peptide Embedding Spaces Using Riemannian Geometry
one_liner: When searching for drug molecules in a compressed space, follow the curved paths the decoder creates instead of pretending the space is flat.
lead: Drug discovery starts with a generative model that squashes a huge space of possible molecules into a compact learned map. But the decoder does not preserve flat Euclidean distances—it bends the space. PepCompass uses that curvature to navigate better: it walks along paths the decoder approves (not random directions), random-walks in directions the decoder recognizes as valid, and proposes mutations the decoder is sensitive to—so all three tools cooperate with the learned structure, finding active antimicrobial peptides that competing flat-space methods miss because they waste steps on bad directions. Real lab validation: 100% hit rate on 25 peptides discovered this way.

paras: Antimicrobial peptides—short chains of amino acids that kill bacteria—are buried in a space so huge (trillions of possibilities) that random testing is hopeless. Researchers train a generative model that learns to map a much smaller latent space (a compact list of learned numbers) onto valid peptides; the decoder (the part that turns numbers into peptide sequences) is trained to reconstruct real peptides.

But here is the trap: most algorithms treat the latent space as flat, like a chessboard. They assume that stepping the same distance in any direction yields the same quality of peptide. In reality, the decoder creates bent, crinkled terrain—some directions yield diverse valid peptides, others are barren, like climbing a valley where some slopes are steep and others are flat. Flat-space navigation ignores these valleys and ridges, sending you up dead-ends.

callout.html: Use the decoder's curvature (how bent the space is at each point) to guide your search, so you walk along geodesics (shortest curves on the bent surface) instead of straight lines through empty space.

steps.text: Learn a decoder that maps learned numbers onto valid peptide sequences.
Search geodesic curves between known good peptides to find promising new seeds.
Take small random steps that respect the bent terrain, not straying into invalid space.
Use the decoder's sensitivity to generate candidate single-amino-acid changes in tangent space.
Apply Bayesian optimization on the enumerated mutations to refine each seed into an active peptide.

paras: The paper replaces flat-space navigation with terrain-aware navigation. Instead of stepping any direction and hoping, you step in directions the decoder's curvature tells you are fruitful. Three tools replace the naive approach: geodesic search (shortest paths on the bent terrain) between known good peptides, random walks that stay on the bent terrain, and mutation enumeration that the decoder approves.

hidden.name: curvature (how bent the terrain is)
paras: The decoder has a Jacobian—a matrix of derivatives showing how sensitive each amino acid at each position is to tiny nudges in latent space. This matrix encodes how the terrain is shaped at that point: where it bends sharply and where it is nearly flat. The paper also computes the Hessian, which measures the second derivatives (how fast the slopes themselves change). In plain terms: it tells you the exact dips and rises of the terrain.

PepCompass estimates this curvature by computing the decoder's second derivatives, then uses those measurements to design its random walks (SORBES) and mutation proposals (MUTANG). A path search (PoGS) minimizes potential energy along a curve, which automatically gives you the shortest path across the bent terrain.

heat.caption: Darker means higher decoder curvature (more bent terrain, richer valid peptides).

reads.html: The decoder bends the latent space, like a curved piece of paper instead of a flat table. PepCompass measures how much each region is bent and uses that measurement to design smarter steps.

The paper computes the Jacobian and Hessian of the decoder (first and second derivatives showing how amino acids respond to nudges) to estimate how bent the terrain is at each latent code. It uses stable numerical techniques to keep calculations reliable.

mechanism.h2: Why bent-terrain navigation finds better peptides
paras: A trained decoder learns the shape of valid peptide space. When you ask it to reconstruct a sequence, its weights encode which latent regions correspond to realistic amino acids. The Jacobian of the decoder tells you the direction and magnitude of that coupling. A high Jacobian in one direction means the decoder is sensitive there—moving even slightly nudges amino acids sharply. A low Jacobian means the decoder is insensitive—you can move far without changing the output.

Path search (PoGS) walks along a curve between two known good peptides, minimizing potential energy. On a flat plane, potential energy is just distance; on bent terrain, it accounts for the slope. This automatically pulls you toward regions where the decoder is stable and varied. Random walks (SORBES) use the curvature to constrain their steps: they wander in directions where the decoder stays on-surface, not plunging into invalid space. Mutation enumeration (MUTANG) uses the Jacobian to propose amino acid swaps that the decoder approves—changes the model is sensitive to, not dead zones. When you combine all three—seeds from paths, local wandering that respects terrain, mutations tailored to decoder sensitivity—you explore efficiently and find more active peptides than flat-space methods.

math.words: total energy along a curve equals sum over all points of (potential function at that point plus motion penalty); minimize this to find the best path
math.equation: E_lambda(Z) = sum_k [ lambda * Phi(p(z_k)) + mu * curvature_penalty ]
symbols: the sequence of latent codes along the curve
index of each point on the curve
the peptide sequence decoded from latent code z_k
the potential (how desirable this peptide is; higher is better)
weight balancing how much we care about the potential
weight on the curvature penalty (smoothness cost)
the roughness of the path (steep ups and downs cost more)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we have three latent codes along a curve: z_0 (seed peptide), z_1 (middle), z_2 (target).
At z_0: potential Phi = 8 (very active peptide), curvature penalty = 0 (starting point).
At z_1: potential Phi = 5 (medium), curvature penalty = 2 (sharp bend costs 2 units).
At z_2: potential Phi = 7 (active target), curvature penalty = 1 (slight bend costs 1).
If we try a path with sharper bends (penalty 5 at z_1), energy rises to 8 + 7.5 + 7.5 = 23, so the smoother path wins.
Minimizing this equation finds the geodesic—the path that balances staying near good peptides with following the decoder's natural curves.

math.note: Geodesic search minimizes this energy, automatically pulling the path toward high-potential regions while keeping it smooth and on-surface.

charts.title: Flat-space baseline (SAASBO/LineBO)
charts.note: Standard latent Bayesian optimization ignores how bent the terrain is, requiring many more exploration steps to find active peptides.

charts.title: PepCompass (terrain-aware)
charts.note: Using path search and random walks that respect bent terrain, every step lands in a region the decoder recognizes as valid, so you waste no steps on dead zones; mutations proposed are ones the decoder is sensitive to, so each test finds active peptides faster. This efficiency yields far more active peptides than flat-space methods.

items.b: Curvature estimation fails on noisy decoders.
items.html: If the decoder is poorly trained or its outputs are noisy, the estimated curvature is wrong, and path searches lead you astray. Random walks will diverge from real high-value regions.

items.b: Computational cost grows with sequence length.
items.html: Estimating the Jacobian and Hessian (second derivatives) for every position in a long peptide becomes slow. The tangent space becomes high-dimensional, and MUTANG enumeration scales poorly.

items.b: Geodesics get trapped in local minima.
items.html: If all nearby seeds lead to mediocre peptides, geodesic search will find only mediocre new seeds. The method escapes this when combined with random walks, but purely global geodesic search is brittle.

items.b: Done right with well-trained decoders and diverse seeds.
items.html: Train the decoder on diverse, real peptides. Start path search from multiple seed pairs covering different regions of latent space. Use random walks to explore freely when you get stuck. Validate all discovered peptides in the lab before deploying.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Train a simple decoder on a toy peptide dataset (or use a pre-trained HydrAMP encoder-decoder). Encode some known active peptides into latent space. Implement path search (PoGS): interpolate between two seed codes, compute the decoder Jacobian at each step, and minimize the energy functional. Then run LE-BO: take the path-search seeds, enumerate mutations via MUTANG, and test each on a simple activity predictor. Compare to a flat-space baseline (Gaussian process or random search in latent space). Measure: how many high-activity peptides do you find per number of decoder calls? How many top-k peptides come from terrain-aware exploration versus flat baseline?
demo.metric_eq: coverage = (fraction of discovered peptides with activity > threshold) / (fraction of tested peptides); compare coverage_PepCompass vs coverage_baseline
demo.closing: A rigorous demo must show that terrain-aware exploration finds more active peptides in fewer steps than treating latent space as flat.
